topics.title: Assertions, tests and useful boundaries
topics.story:
An elevator inspector does not only ride from floor two to floor three on a quiet day. They test the ground floor, top floor, empty cabin, capacity limit and invalid requests, because boundaries reveal mistakes ordinary trips can hide. Software tests follow the same logic. A warning light inside the maintenance panel resembles a language assertion: valuable for detecting internal assumptions, but unsuitable as the only protection against a passenger selecting an impossible destination.

Public validation must work during normal operation, whether diagnostic assertions are enabled or disabled.
topics.principle:
A test checks observed behavior against an expected result. Derive cases from the contract: normal cases, boundaries, invalid inputs and relevant state transitions. Black-box tests use public behavior; white-box reasoning can identify untested branches without making tests depend on every implementation detail.

Java's assert statement can be disabled, so it is useful for internal consistency checks but should not be the sole validation of public input. Testing frameworks such as JUnit provide assertions that execute as part of tests independently of the Java assert switch. Keep each test understandable and deterministic, and verify exceptional behavior as well as normal returns.

Passing tests increase confidence for the covered cases but are not a proof that no defects remain.
topics.symbols:
Arrange establishes the initial conditions, Act invokes the behavior under test, and Assert compares observations with the contract. m is the largest accepted input in a simple contiguous integer range. The boundary set samples just outside and exactly on its edges; other values are still needed when the logic has additional branches.

Expected behavior can include unchanged state after rejection. Coverage statistics count execution, not the quality of the expectations being checked.
topics.example:
A booking object has 8 seats and currently holds 3 reservations. Test reserve(2): the resulting reserved count should be 5. In an independent fixture, test reserve(5): the result should be 8. Test reserve(6): it should reject the request and keep the count at 3. Also test a negative request and decide from the documented contract whether zero is valid.

These cases exercise ordinary success, exact capacity, overflow of capacity and invalid sign. Reusing a mutated fixture carelessly can make the second test depend on the first, so each case should establish its own starting state.
topics.pitfall: A test that merely repeats the implementation's calculation can repeat its bug. Choose expectations from the contract, a simple independent example or a known invariant.

check.question: Why is assert amount > 0 insufficient to validate an externally supplied removal amount?
check.answer: Java assertions may be disabled. The program must use an ordinary conditional and appropriate exception or error response to enforce a public input requirement reliably.

glossary.meaning: The prepared objects and inputs for one test case.
An input on or near a rule’s acceptance limit.
A retained test that detects a previously understood defect returning.

guided_questions.question: Why create a fresh object for each reservation test?
guided_questions.answer: Otherwise one test’s mutation changes the next test’s starting state. Independent fixtures make each expected result interpretable.

guided_questions.question: Why not rely on Java assert for public validation?
guided_questions.answer: The assert statement can be disabled. A normal conditional and exception always enforce the input contract.

guided_questions.question: Does branch coverage prove expected values are correct?
guided_questions.answer: No. It records execution. A test must still compare meaningful observations with an independently derived expectation.

instructor_notes.title: Test the rejection guarantee too
instructor_notes.body: An exception may be correct while the object was wrongly mutated first. After catching the expected failure, check the documented remaining state.

instructor_notes.title: Use a discriminating numeric case
instructor_notes.body: An average of [2,4] is an integer, so an integer-division bug can pass. [3,6] expects 4.5 and exposes the defect with a tiny understandable case.

code_examples.title: Run boundary tests without a test dependency
code_examples.intro: The local check method always runs, regardless of the Java assert switch.
code_examples.output: four contract cases passed
code_examples.explanation:
Every helper constructs a fresh fixture starting at three reserved seats. Success cases check ordinary and exact-capacity results. Rejection cases check both the exception and unchanged state.

The harness throws AssertionError if an expectation fails. It is an original small test harness, not the Java assert statement or a replacement for all features of a test framework.
walkthrough: Arrange a new fixture inside each test helper.
Act once with a normal, exact-boundary, or invalid request.
Check resulting values and rejection-state guarantees.

syntax_notes.meaning: Create a fresh fixture with capacity eight and starting occupancy three.
Use an always-active check. ! negates the boolean; this is not the optionally disabled assert statement.
Catch the failure required by the test case. The variable name expected documents that role.

code_examples.title: Keep a focused arithmetic regression test
code_examples.intro: Show why a fractional expected result detects integer division.
code_examples.output:
fractional average=4.5
empty input rejected=true
code_examples.explanation:
The expected 4.5 comes from the independent calculation (3+6)/2. Converting sum before division preserves that fraction. Equality is safe for this exactly representable half, not a universal rule for floating-point tests.

The empty case checks a separate contract branch. The method assumes a non-null array and uses a long sum to widen accumulation.
walkthrough: Choose a case whose correct answer is not an integer.
Check the return independently of the implementation’s intermediate arithmetic.
Test empty-input rejection separately.

topics.title: Recursion, call trees and reusable results
topics.story:
A nested set of folders can be counted by asking each folder for the sizes of its children, then adding one for itself. Every request handles a smaller part of the structure, and an empty folder stops the descent. Now suppose several routes ask for the same expensive calculation. A clerk can record an answer the first time and reuse it, but only if the recorded answer corresponds to the same inputs and assumptions.

These two pictures separate recursion, which breaks a problem into smaller calls, from memoization, which avoids repeating equivalent work.
topics.principle:
A recursive method needs base cases and recursive calls that make progress toward them. Each active call has its own locals and contributes to call-stack depth. Correctness can be argued by assuming smaller instances work and showing how their results combine into the current answer. Recursive traversal of object structures also needs a policy for cycles and repeated references; a tree assumption is not automatically true of an arbitrary object graph.

Memoization caches results by the inputs that determine them. It helps when subproblems repeat, but uses memory and can become incorrect if relevant state changes without invalidation. Deep recursion can overflow the Java stack even when the mathematical algorithm terminates. Consider iterative alternatives when depth can be large.
topics.formula:
ways(0) = 1; ways(1) = 1
ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2), n ≥ 2
Memoized states: n+1; time O(n), storage O(n) for this recurrence
topics.symbols:
ways(n) counts sequences of one-step and two-step moves covering exactly n steps, where n is a nonnegative integer. There is one empty sequence for zero steps. The time bound assumes each cached state is computed once and arithmetic is constant cost, which holds only while values fit the chosen fixed-width type.

Recursive memoization additionally uses O(n) call-stack space in the worst case. Large exact answers need wider or arbitrary-precision arithmetic, changing the arithmetic cost model.
topics.example:
For a staircase of 4 steps, ways(2) = 1 + 1 = 2, ways(3) = 2 + 1 = 3, and ways(4) = 3 + 2 = 5. The five patterns are 1111, 112, 121, 211 and 22. A direct recursive evaluation recomputes ways(2) from multiple branches. With a cache, compute each of ways(0) through ways(4) once and reuse the stored result. Reject negative n or define a deliberate alternate contract.

For n large enough to overflow int, correct recursion still produces incorrect numeric results unless the representation is changed.
topics.pitfall: A cache key must include every input that affects the result. Caching by n alone is wrong if another configurable rule changes the allowed step sizes.

check.question: Why does memoization not automatically solve a StackOverflowError?
check.answer: It reduces repeated computation but may leave the longest chain of recursive calls unchanged. An iterative dynamic program can avoid that deep call chain.

glossary.meaning: A case answered without another recursive call.
Caching a result under the inputs that determine it.
The number of simultaneously active nested calls.

guided_questions.question: Why is ways(0) one?
guided_questions.answer: There is one empty sequence of moves covering zero steps. This base case makes the recurrence count combinations correctly.

guided_questions.question: What does memoization remove?
guided_questions.answer: Repeated evaluation of the same state. It does not necessarily shorten the longest dependency chain or prevent deep-stack failure.

guided_questions.question: Why must a cache key include the allowed step rule?
guided_questions.answer: Changing allowed moves can change the answer for the same n. A cache indexed only by n is valid only while that rule stays fixed.

instructor_notes.title: Count subproblems before optimizing
instructor_notes.body: For this recurrence only states zero through n are needed. Caching makes each state compute once, but an iterative recurrence can also retain just the two preceding values.

instructor_notes.title: Arithmetic size changes complexity
instructor_notes.body: BigInteger avoids fixed-width overflow but its additions cost more as values grow. The number of recurrence steps may be linear while total bit-operation cost is not constant per step.

code_examples.title: Cache each staircase state once
code_examples.intro: Count distinct computations, then repeat the same query.
code_examples.output:
ways(4)=5
computed states=5
repeat=5
computed after repeat=5
code_examples.explanation:
The cache is checked before work is counted. Each missing state computes its answer and stores it, including the two base cases. The first query reaches five distinct states, zero through four.

The repeated query returns the cached value without increasing the count. The explicit range keeps answers within long; checked addition still makes unexpected overflow visible.
walkthrough: Check the base contract and cache before recursion.
Combine smaller states and cache the computed result.
Repeat the query to verify reuse rather than repeated work.

syntax_notes.meaning: Associate each input state with its computed result; wrappers allow both numeric types as generic arguments.
Distinguish an existing cached result from an absent mapping in this chosen cache representation.
Add long values and throw if the result overflows, rather than silently wrapping.

code_examples.title: Replace deep recursion with an iterative exact count
code_examples.intro: Use BigInteger and two rolling states for a larger input.
code_examples.explanation:
Before each loop step, previous and current hold the two preceding recurrence values. A temporary next prevents overwriting a value before both are used. No recursive calls remain.

BigInteger keeps the count exact beyond long range. Only two recurrence values are retained, but their storage grows with the number of digits. The explicit demonstration limit keeps execution bounded.
walkthrough: Initialize both base recurrence values to one.
Compute next before shifting the rolling pair.
Print small boundary checks and one larger exact result.

topics.title: Anonymous classes, lambdas and captured context
topics.story:
A café needs a small rule for deciding which orders receive a reminder. It could hire a named specialist for every rule, but a short written instruction passed to the reminder system is often clearer. That instruction still needs a known format: what input it receives and what answer it returns. A lambda fills such a single-operation contract.

An anonymous class is closer to a temporary worker with their own identity and potentially additional internal state. Both avoid a separate named class, but they do not create identical scoping or identity behavior.
topics.principle:
An anonymous class expression constructs an instance of a class declared at that point, extending one class or implementing one interface. A lambda supplies an implementation for a functional interface, whose abstract method contract has one functional operation after the language's inheritance and Object-method rules are considered.

Default and static methods do not themselves add abstract obligations. Parameter and return types must match the target interface. Lambdas can capture local variables only when those variables are final or effectively final. Capturing a reference does not freeze the referenced object. In a lambda, this refers to the enclosing instance; in an anonymous class, this refers to the anonymous-class instance.

Use named methods or classes when behavior becomes too complex to read locally.
topics.formula:
Predicate<T>: T → boolean
Function<T,R>: T → R
Example: length -> length >= minimum
Captured local variables must be final or effectively final
topics.symbols:
T is an input reference type and R is a result type. The arrows describe function-shaped contracts, not a promise that every implementation is pure or free of side effects. minimum is a local variable whose value cannot be reassigned after capture in the enclosing method. A block lambda uses an explicit return when returning a value from statements.

The interface determines the target type; the lambda expression does not stand alone as an untyped universal function.
topics.example:
A reminder system uses Predicate<Integer> overdue = days -> days >= 3. Testing days 1, 3 and 5 gives false, true and true. If the threshold comes from int minimum = 3, the lambda can capture it provided the local variable is not later reassigned. A final List<String> log can also be captured, and log.add can mutate the list: final constrains the reference, not the list contents.

To change the rule deliberately, construct a new predicate using a new threshold. Avoid hiding changing domain state inside a captured mutable object unless the surrounding design clearly requires it.
topics.pitfall: A lambda is not simply an anonymous class with shorter spelling. Their this binding differs, and a lambda requires a functional-interface target rather than any arbitrary abstract class.

check.question: Can an interface with one abstract method and two default methods be a lambda target?
check.answer: Yes, assuming it satisfies the full functional-interface rules. Default methods already have implementations and do not add required abstract operations.

glossary.meaning: An interface with one abstract method that supplies a lambda’s target type.
Using a value or reference from the surrounding scope in a lambda.
A local variable assigned once and never reassigned after initialization.

guided_questions.question: Does a lambda freeze the object it captures?
guided_questions.answer: No. The captured reference cannot be reassigned locally, but the referred object can still be mutable.

guided_questions.question: When does a lambda body run?
guided_questions.answer: When the functional method is called, not simply when the lambda is created.

guided_questions.question: What does this mean inside a lambda?
guided_questions.answer: It keeps the meaning from the enclosing instance context. An anonymous class introduces its own instance instead.

instructor_notes.title: Prefer explicit data when behavior travels
instructor_notes.body: Capturing mutable collections makes later behavior depend on later state. Pass immutable snapshots when a delayed operation must describe the original moment.

instructor_notes.title: A concise body still has a contract
instructor_notes.body: A Predicate should normally answer a question without surprising mutations. Side effects in a filtering predicate complicate reuse, testing and parallel execution.

code_examples.title: Capture a threshold and a mutable log
code_examples.intro: Distinguish a fixed local reference from a frozen object.
code_examples.output:
oak accepted=true
ox accepted=false
log size=0
log size=1
code_examples.explanation:
The threshold local is never reassigned, so it can be captured. Calling test supplies the missing String input. Creation alone does not inspect any string.

The report lambda captures the log reference. Both calls reach the same list, whose contents change between calls. Effectively final restricts local assignment; it does not make the list immutable.
walkthrough: Create a predicate using an unchanged threshold local.
Call test with two explicit inputs.
Mutate the captured list and call the same report again.

syntax_notes.meaning: Name one parameter s; the expression after the arrow supplies the boolean result.
Use the standard functional interface whose test method accepts String and returns boolean.
Empty parentheses mean no parameters. The body runs only when the functional method is invoked.

code_examples.title: See which object this names
code_examples.intro: Run a lambda and an anonymous Runnable from the same enclosing instance.
code_examples.output:
lambda=outer
anonymous=inner
enclosing=outer
code_examples.explanation:
The lambda belongs to the lexical context of Presenter.show, so this.name finds the Presenter field. The anonymous object has its own name field and its own this.

Presenter.this explicitly selects the enclosing instance from the anonymous class. This distinction matters when converting callbacks: shorter syntax can change what an unqualified this refers to.
walkthrough: Create an enclosing Presenter instance.
Run the lambda and resolve this in the enclosing context.
Run the anonymous object and distinguish its own field from the enclosing field.

topics.title: Debugging with evidence and documenting promises
topics.story:
A mechanic investigates a bicycle that clicks once per wheel rotation. Replacing every component at once may stop the sound, but it reveals little about the cause. Instead, the mechanic reproduces the click, observes where it begins, forms a narrow explanation and checks it. Debugging should preserve the same discipline.

Documentation is the maintenance card explaining what the bicycle is supposed to do and under what conditions. Together, a reproducible observation and a stated contract distinguish an implementation defect from a mistaken expectation about the program's intended behavior.
topics.principle:
Separate compile errors, runtime exceptions and incorrect results. First reproduce a defect with the smallest useful input, then compare expected and actual behavior at an appropriate boundary. A debugger can pause at breakpoints, inspect locals and call stacks, step into a method or step over it, and reveal the earliest divergence.

Compilation with debugging information improves inspection; the exact commands depend on the tool. Fix the cause and retain a focused regression test when the behavior warrants one. Javadoc documents public contracts using descriptions and tags such as @param, @return and @throws. Explain assumptions, side effects, units and exceptional behavior.

Comments that merely repeat a method name are weaker than a precise statement of what callers may rely on.
topics.formula:
Reproduce → observe → hypothesis → targeted check → correction
Contract = accepted inputs + promised outputs + side effects + failure behavior
topics.symbols:
The arrows represent an investigation loop: a failed hypothesis sends you back to observation. Accepted inputs include ranges, null handling and units; promised outputs include ordering or state guarantees when relevant. Side effects identify mutations or external I/O. Failure behavior describes exceptions and what remains true after failure.

These are conceptual categories, not a mathematical equation. Documentation and tests should agree on the same contract so that a failing test has an interpretable meaning.
topics.example:
A method calculating average delivery time returns 4.0 for durations [3, 6], although the expected result is 4.5. Reproduce the issue with just these two values. At a breakpoint, inspect sum = 9 and count = 2; both are correct. Step to the division and observe 9 / 2 evaluated as int before assignment to double.

The narrow fix is to convert an operand before division. Add a test with a nonintegral average and document the empty-input behavior. Testing only [2, 4] would have missed the defect because integer division happens to give the expected whole result.
topics.pitfall: Do not change several unrelated conditions before checking a hypothesis. Do not document a non-null precondition while silently accepting null in one path and crashing unpredictably in another.

check.question: Why is a breakpoint just before the wrong output sometimes too late to understand the defect?
check.answer: The bad state may have been created much earlier. Trace backward to where an invariant first became false, then observe the operation that caused that first divergence.

glossary.meaning: A small input and program that reliably reveal a failure.
A specific explanation that predicts an observable result.
A requirement that must hold when a method is called.

guided_questions.question: Why inspect operand types before changing a formula?
guided_questions.answer: The written formula may be correct while the language evaluates an intermediate operation in the wrong numeric domain.

guided_questions.question: What should documentation promise?
guided_questions.answer: Observable behavior: accepted inputs, returned meaning, state effects and expected failures. Avoid promising accidental implementation details.

guided_questions.question: Is a print statement a proof?
guided_questions.answer: It is evidence from one execution. Use it to test a hypothesis, then retain a focused regression check.

instructor_notes.title: Reduce one variable at a time
instructor_notes.body: A tiny reproducer separates arithmetic from file input, graphics and unrelated state. If the failure disappears, restore the last removed condition and investigate its role.

instructor_notes.title: Make comments explain the reason
instructor_notes.body: A useful comment records why a guard or conversion is necessary. Repeating each statement in prose adds maintenance work without explaining the contract.

code_examples.title: Locate the first wrong intermediate value
code_examples.intro: Compare the same arithmetic with conversion at two different positions.
code_examples.output:
integer quotient=4
late conversion=4.0
early conversion=4.5
code_examples.explanation:
Start with the known answer 9/2 = 4.5. The integer quotient is already 4, so the loss occurs before conversion. Casting that result cannot reconstruct the discarded fraction.

Casting one operand first changes the division to floating point. This tiny test separates the type error from input and output code, and retains a check for this exactly representable result.

Inspect the value immediately after integer division.
Move the conversion before division and retain the regression check.

Convert one operand before division, so the division uses floating point.
Check inequality against an independent expected result. This particular half is exactly representable.

code_examples.title: Turn documentation into executable checks
code_examples.intro: Document a small method and exercise both accepted and rejected inputs.

distance=7
rejected negative position
code_examples.explanation:
The comment describes the accepted domain, returned meaning and rejection condition. It does not require a particular local variable name or branch order.

The guard enforces the stated domain before arithmetic. Widening the left operand makes subtraction use long, so this implementation also avoids int subtraction overflow if the domain is later broadened. Such a domain change still needs new tests and documentation.
walkthrough: Read the contract before predicting the output.
Check a valid pair and its returned distance.
Check rejection at the documented negative boundary.

topics.title: From object model to a small event-driven application
topics.story:
A community greenhouse has sensors, a control policy and a wall display. If the display itself decides every watering rule, changing screen layout can accidentally change plant care. Instead, the greenhouse model stores current conditions, the policy updates them, and the display shows a snapshot. Button presses become requests to that model.

This separation also makes a useful paper diagram: boxes show responsibilities and links show collaboration. The diagram is valuable only when it helps explain behavior, not when it reproduces every field and method without showing why the parts belong together.
topics.principle:
A small application benefits from explicit responsibilities. Keep domain state and rules in model objects; keep input parsing or event handling at a boundary; let presentation read state without owning unrelated domain decisions. UML class diagrams can summarize fields, operations, visibility and relationships: a generalization arrow describes inheritance, realization describes interface implementation, and association describes collaboration.

Composition expresses a strong ownership relationship, not every reference field. Packages organize names and accessibility; build tools automate compilation, dependency resolution and repeatable checks. In an event-driven program, handlers translate events into model operations, and rendering reads the resulting state.

Separate logical updates from display timing so the same behavior can be tested without requiring a graphical window.
topics.formula:
event → validated command → model transition → render state
State after command = update(previous state, command)
Design review: one clear responsibility per component; explicit collaboration
topics.symbols:
An event is a raw interaction such as a button press. A validated command is a domain-level request with checked inputs. update denotes the model's transition logic; it may be implemented with mutable objects or returned state, provided the contract is clear. render converts state into a view and should not secretly advance unrelated domain rules.

The responsibility guideline is a design heuristic, not a numerical law or a demand that every class contain only one method.
topics.example:
Design a greenhouse dashboard with a Bed model storing moisture, a WateringPolicy deciding whether watering is allowed, and a Dashboard rendering current values. A button event requests addWater(2) for a particular bed. The handler identifies the bed, the model validates the amount and updates moisture, and the display refreshes from the new state.

For a simplified model measured in moisture units, a unit test starts at 4, adds 2 and checks the result 6 without opening a window. A class diagram shows Dashboard associated with Bed and the policy interface, while a concrete policy realizes that interface. The same collaboration can be exercised through a headless command interface before adding a graphical view.
topics.pitfall: Avoid one application class that performs parsing, storage, drawing and every domain rule. Also avoid adding layers without a responsibility they actually clarify.

check.question: What becomes easier when display code reads model state but does not own the domain rules?
check.answer: The rules can be tested and reused independently of the interface. A command-line view or a different graphical view can call the same model operations without duplicating their logic.

glossary.meaning: The data and rules that represent the application’s domain.
The place where an external action becomes a validated domain request.
Passing a collaborator into an object instead of constructing a fixed one internally.

guided_questions.question: Why keep rules outside a button callback?
guided_questions.answer: The same rules can be tested and reused without opening a window. The callback then translates an event into a request.

guided_questions.question: Who decides whether watering is allowed?
guided_questions.answer: The model or an explicit policy should enforce that rule. A disabled button alone does not protect other callers.

guided_questions.question: Does separating layers require many classes?
guided_questions.answer: No. Begin with distinct responsibilities and clear method contracts. Add classes when ownership or interchangeable behavior makes that useful.

guided_questions.question: Why compute the result before pushing history?
guided_questions.answer: The operation can reject the input. If history changes first, Undo may restore an identical snapshot and appear to do nothing. Validate before committing the state change.

instructor_notes.title: Headless tests shorten the feedback loop
instructor_notes.body: Testing the model directly makes failures reproducible and fast. A separate small integration test can check that event translation and rendering connect correctly.

instructor_notes.title: Inject policy before adding branches everywhere
instructor_notes.body: If different environments need different watering rules, represent the variation as one policy. Keep invariant checks in the model even when the policy recommends an action.

code_examples.title: Follow a command through a small application
code_examples.intro: Keep input translation, domain state and rendering as separate methods.
code_examples.output:
water 2 -> accepted
moisture=6
water 8 -> rejected
moisture=6
water many -> rejected
moisture=6
code_examples.explanation:
The command handler recognizes a tiny grammar and converts its numeric argument. Bed owns the range rule and changes state only after validation. Render reads the resulting state without changing it.

The excessive request and malformed number are rejected through the same user-facing boundary. They leave moisture at six. This headless sequence checks coordination without a graphical toolkit.
walkthrough: Translate each command into one validated model request.
Let the model enforce its own capacity rule.
Render after both success and failure to verify preserved state.

syntax_notes.meaning: Split this deliberately small command grammar at single spaces into an array of fields.
Translate a numeric text field into an int, rejecting malformed or out-of-range text.
Build a view string by concatenation. Reading this field does not advance the model.

code_examples.title: Replace one policy without rewriting the controller
code_examples.intro: Pass a target rule as behavior and enforce the model bound independently.
code_examples.output:
gentle=6
dry day=8
unsafe policy rejected
code_examples.explanation:
Both policies implement the same contract: inspect current moisture and suggest an amount. The shared apply method asks the selected policy and validates its answer before computing the new state.

An injected collaborator can still be wrong. The final example deliberately recommends twenty units, and the independent range check rejects it. Policy flexibility does not replace invariant enforcement.
walkthrough: Express each target rule as an IntUnaryOperator.
Pass the chosen policy into one shared application function.
Reject a policy result that would violate the model boundary.

code_examples.title: Build a small editor with undo
code_examples.intro: Mina writes labels for a school exhibition. She adds a word, notices a mistake, and wants Undo. Saving only the newest text loses the previous state. She separates the document from the editing action and lets the editor keep a stack of snapshots. She also decides that a rejected action must not enter the history. Now she can test the editor without building any buttons.
code_examples.output:
Hello Python
rejected without history
undo: Hello
walkthrough: Edit describes an operation. Append implements one operation; Editor does not need to know how the new text is produced.
Compute and validate next before changing history or text. An ordinary rejected edit leaves both unchanged.
push records the old text. pop restores the most recent snapshot, which is last-in, first-out behavior.
Test an empty undo, two successful edits, one failed edit, and a final undo. A failed edit must not consume an undo step.
code_examples.explanation:
A state transition is text_next = edit(text_current). The history stores earlier text_current values. String objects are immutable, so keeping their references preserves snapshots without cloning their characters at every push. Creating each concatenated result still costs time and memory proportional to its length. Keeping many long snapshots can therefore use substantial memory.

Build in four stages: define a valid document, add one operation, add history, then connect a user interface. A button should call execute; it should not maintain a second copy of the document. This keeps tests independent of screen events.

The Edit contract here assumes the operation only computes text and does not perform external side effects. Undoing a string cannot undo an email or a file write. This simple editor has no redo, persistence or concurrent edits. For large documents, consider storing inverse edits or using a persistent text structure after measuring the need.

syntax_notes.meaning: Name the behavior the editor needs.
A double-ended queue used here as a stack of snapshots.
Reject an invalid operation before committing a new state.

cheatsheet.title: Compilation is one check
cheatsheet.body: Compile-time type checks do not prove intended behavior. Trace numeric conversions, handle runtime failures and test the contract, especially integer division, overflow and empty inputs.

cheatsheet.title: Java passes values
cheatsheet.body: A method receives copies of argument values. A copied reference can reach shared mutable state; reassigning the parameter never reassigns the caller’s variable.

cheatsheet.title: Array boundaries
cheatsheet.body: For a non-null array, valid indices satisfy 0 ≤ i < length. A multidimensional array can have null or unequal-length rows; an outer clone is shallow.

cheatsheet.title: Identity and equality
cheatsheet.body: Use == for reference identity and enum constants; use equals for value equality when the class defines it. Equal objects must have equal hash codes; the reverse implication is false.

cheatsheet.title: Preserve invariants
cheatsheet.body: Construct valid objects and check each operation before invalid state escapes. private and final help, but neither automatically makes a referenced object immutable.

cheatsheet.title: Two method-selection stages
cheatsheet.body: Compile-time argument types select an overload. The runtime receiver chooses an overridden instance implementation. Static methods hide, and changing only a return type does not create an overload.

cheatsheet.title: Choose by collection contract
cheatsheet.body: List preserves order and duplicates, Set models uniqueness, and Map associates keys with values. Compare lookup, insertion and traversal costs rather than assuming one implementation is universally faster.

cheatsheet.title: Generic data flow
cheatsheet.body: Generics are invariant. Use ? extends T for a source of T and ? super T for a destination of T. These are type guarantees, not complete immutability guarantees.

cheatsheet.title: Failure and cleanup
cheatsheet.body: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared. Catch where recovery is meaningful, retain the cause, and use try-with-resources for owned resources. Garbage collection does not replace timely resource cleanup.

cheatsheet.title: Tests and recursion
cheatsheet.body: Test normal cases, boundaries and rejection state. Recursive code also needs a base case and decreasing problem size; memoization avoids repeated states but may leave deep call stacks.

cheatsheet.title: Lambda context
cheatsheet.body: A lambda needs a functional-interface target and captures final or effectively final locals. Captured objects may remain mutable; lambda this refers to the enclosing instance.

cheatsheet.title: Design and diagnose
cheatsheet.body: Separate model rules, event input and rendering. Reproduce defects, inspect the earliest divergence, test a specific hypothesis, and document accepted inputs, effects, outputs and failure behavior.
